title: Traer --- Bringing, and Latin for Dragging

lessons.title: traer — "to bring", and the direction baked into it
lessons.gloss: to bring — Latin's word for dragging, and a verb with a direction built into it

segments.text: Me levanto, and now estoy de pie. Up, and carrying something. The verb for that has a direction inside it that English leaves open.
r-tap — one flick of the tongue: tra-ER, two beats.
g-hard — the g of traigo is hard, as in English go.
traer ("to bring") from Latin trahere, "to drag, to pull". Bringing started out as hauling.

Latin built a second stem, tract-, and English helped itself to both: tractor, traction, attract, contract, subtract, extract, distract, retract — and abstract, abs- + trahere, something "dragged away" from anything particular.
Then the worn-down half, through French: trace, train (what is dragged along behind), trail, portray from prōtrahere, "to draw forth", and retreat from retrahere, "to draw back".

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the hard g, for the second time

segments.text: Oír grew a hard -g- in oigo and nowhere else in its present. Traer does the identical thing: traigo, and then four ordinary -er endings. One club, two members so far, and neither one announces itself.

blocks.title: Why it's said this way: here, or away

segments.text: English lets one verb wander: bring me the bread, bring it to the café — same word, opposite journeys. Spanish will not.

Traer moves a thing toward you. Llevar moves it away. Traigo el pan is the bread arriving here; llevo el pan is the bread leaving with me. You choose by where you are standing, never by what you are carrying.
And llevar from Latin levāre, "to raise" — the verb already behind levantarse. To carry a load was first to lift it.

segments.instruction: "Traigo el pan" then "Llevo el pan" — here, then away
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "Traigo el pan" then "Llevo el pan" — here, then away]
[YOU SAY: "oigo" then "traigo" — the same hard g]

segments.text: Which way does traer carry a thing, and which verb goes the other way? (Toward you; llevar.) What did trahere mean, and name two English words from it. (To drag; tractor, attract, abstract, retreat.) Which form of traer misbehaves, and which verb showed you that same misbehaviour first? (Traigo; oigo.) And say you are standing. (Estoy de pie.)
